radar.title: Interference-Graph-Aided Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning for Beam Hopping LEO Satellite Networks
radar.summary: Beam hopping technology enables LEO satellites to dynamically switch beam coverage positions, providing flexible resource allocation for non-uniformly distributed traffic demands. However, the severe spatial interference coupling among beams makes coordinated scheduling challenging. To address this problem, in this letter, we propose an interference-graph-aided multi-agent reinforcement learning approach that constructs an interference graph to capture beam coupling relationships and injects this structural prior into agent-side representation learning. Each beam agent aggregates information from interference neighbors via graph convolution before estimating local Q-values, which are then decomposed by the standard mixing network. Simulation results demonstrate that the proposed method achieves 34.4\% higher throughput than QMIX with more stable interference management, under non-uniform traffic and co-channel interference settings.

radar.title: Finite-Time Minimax Bounds and an Optimal Lyapunov Policy in Queueing Control
radar.summary: Finite-Time Guarantees for Scheduling Scheduling underpins modern infrastructure, including data centers, wireless networks, service systems, and graphics processing unit clusters. In these environments, bursty, nonstationary demand and stringent service objectives call for rigorous finite-time performance guarantees. In “Finite-Time Minimax Bounds and an Optimal Lyapunov Policy in Queueing Control,” Liu, Tan, and Xu develop a minimax framework for analyzing finite-time scheduling performance. The framework quantitatively characterizes how the expected total queue length scales with system capacity and variability in arrivals and departures, providing a basis for evaluating and comparing scheduling policies. The authors also introduce LyapOpt, which accounts for both first- and second-order effects in service allocation, whereas MaxWeight optimizes only first-order drift. Under a specific structured condition, LyapOpt achieves optimal finite-time performance while retaining stability guarantees. In contrast, MaxWeight’s finite-time performance scales suboptimally with system parameters. These results clarify the limitations of classical drift-based scheduling and motivate new queueing-control methods with rigorous finite-time guarantees.

radar.title: Prophet Inequalities for a New Class of Overbooking Problems in Container Shipping
radar.summary: A New Class of Overbooking Problems in Container Shipping Industry Container carriers lose billions of dollars each year when shippers reserve slots but fail to show up with the corresponding cargo. This paper studies an online booking problem under a deposit-based mechanism designed to better align incentives and mitigate the costs of overbooking. The authors derive near-optimal online policies for two demand settings: one in which shippers’ no-show behavior is coupled through a spot market, and another in which no-shows are independent. In the coupled setting, a randomized threshold policy guarantees at least 81.9% of clairvoyant profit. In the independent setting, a simple greedy policy is shown to be asymptotically 0.5-optimal as the number of slots tends to infinity. Extensive simulations further demonstrate strong and robust practical performance.

radar.title: Uniform-Price Mechanism Design for Automated Market Makers
radar.summary: Automated market makers (AMMs) are central to decentralized exchanges, but their reserve curves make mechanism design different from classical double auctions. We study a batch double auction with buyers, sellers, and a liquidity-nondecreasing AMM: post-trade reserves must have weakly larger product than the initial reserves. Each user has two-dimensional private information: a unit value and a demand or supply quantity. User trades clear at one uniform price subject to AMM feasibility. The objective is user-side trading volume, benchmarked against the optimal feasible individually rational (IR) uniform-price allocation. We give a randomized uniform-price mechanism based on binary quantity buckets. It randomly chooses one of three clearing modes: peer-to-peer matching, AMM sales to buyers, and seller sales to the AMM. Every deterministic realization of the mechanism is ex-post feasible and satisfies IR and weak quantity incentive compatibility: conditional on any quantity report, truthful unit-value reporting is dominant whenever it gives a non-negative utility, no unit-value deviation gives a positive utility if the truthful one doesn't, and users cannot benefit by under-reporting the quantity together with their truthful unit value. Let $V^\ast$ be the optimal feasible IR uniform-price volume without incentive constraints, and let $γ=\bar q/\underline q$, where $\bar q$ and $\underline q$ are the quantity-domain bounds. For $γ\ge1$, the mechanism achieves an expected trading volume of $ Ω(1/(1+\logγ)^2)V^\ast - O(\bar q). $ We also show that full incentive compatibility over the two-dimensional type space forces a worst-case approximation ratio of $O(1/γ)$ at every prescribed initial reserve ratio, even when both AMM reserves are scaled by an arbitrarily large common factor and the optimal volume $V^\ast$ is arbitrarily large relative to $\bar q$.

radar.title: Hardness Amplification for Approximate Nash Equilibrium with Constantly Many Players
radar.summary: For every fixed $\varepsilon\in(0,1)$ and $η\in[0,1)$, we prove that computing an $(\varepsilon,η)$-weak approximate Nash equilibrium requires quasipolynomial time assuming deterministic PPAD-ETH, even in symmetric binary-payoff games with a constant number of players. The games are given by complete payoff tables, and the player count depends only on the tolerances. The weak approximate Nash equilibrium allows at most an $η$ fraction of players to gain more than $\varepsilon$ by deviating unilaterally. The main technical result is an unconditional error-amplification reduction from bimatrix games. For every fixed $δ\in(0,1)$, it transforms a rational bimatrix game with payoffs in $[0,1]$ into a symmetric binary-payoff game with a polynomial-size complete table and a player count depending only on $δ,\varepsilon,η$. Every $(\varepsilon,η)$-weak approximate equilibrium of the constructed game yields a $δ$-approximate Nash equilibrium of the bimatrix game. Construction and recovery take polynomial time in their explicit inputs. Combining this reduction with the bimatrix hardness result of Rubinstein [FOCS 16] gives a deterministic worst-case running-time lower bound of $N^{(\log N)^{1-o(1)}}$, where $N$ is the constructed table's binary encoding length.

radar.title: Group size effects and collective misalignment in LLM multi-agent systems

radar.summary: Multi-agent systems of large language models (LLMs) are rapidly expanding across domains, introducing dynamics not captured by single-agent evaluations. Yet, existing work has mostly contrasted the behavior of a single agent with that of a collective of fixed size, leaving open a central question: How does group size shape dynamics? Here, we move beyond this dichotomy and systematically explore outcomes across the full range of group sizes. We focus on multi-agent misalignment, building on recent evidence that interacting LLMs playing a simple coordination game can generate collective biases absent in individual models. First, we show that collective bias is a deeper phenomenon than previously assessed: Interaction can amplify individual biases, introduce new ones, or override model-level preferences. Second, we demonstrate that group size affects the dynamics in a nonlinear way, revealing model-dependent dynamical regimes. Finally, we develop a mean-field analytical approach and show that, above a critical population size, simulations converge to deterministic predictions that expose the basins of attraction of competing equilibria. These findings establish group size as a key driver of multi-agent dynamics and highlight the need to consider population-level effects when deploying LLM-based systems at scale.

radar.title: Role-Guided Risk-Aware Attention for Multi-AUV Target-Zone Reaching under Active Defense
radar.summary: Cooperative target-zone reaching by multiple autonomous underwater vehicles (AUVs) under active defense remains challenging because each vehicle must make sequential guidance decisions under nonlinear hydrodynamics, sonar-limited perception, obstacle constraints, and defender interference. This paper proposes a role-guided risk-aware attention variant of multi-agent deep deterministic policy gradient (MADDPG), termed role-guided risk-aware attention MADDPG (RGRA-MADDPG), for attacker-side multi-AUV target-zone reaching under active defense. Different from homogeneous multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) policies, the proposed method assigns mission-specific roles to the AUVs, including a Primary Attack AUV, a Coordinated Strike AUV, and a Bait AUV. A role-conditioned attention module is developed to help each AUV selectively emphasize targets, defenders, obstacles, and teammates from local observations, while a risk-prior bias introduces interpretable obstacle-, defender-, and target-related cues into the attention scores. The framework is trained under centralized training and executed through decentralized local policies. Comparative simulations, perturbation tests, mechanism-isolation studies, and physical-response validation are used to evaluate target-reaching success, cooperative behavior, robustness, and command feasibility. Results show that the proposed method improves adversarial target-zone reaching performance over standard MADDPG-based variants while producing differentiated and interpretable multi-AUV tactics.

radar.title: Fixed Sets and the Hardness of Computing Correlated Equilibria
radar.summary: We show that computing an approximate correlated equilibrium of a polytope game is PPAD-complete, and thus polynomial-time equivalent to finding a Nash equilibrium. This challenges the conventional view in game theory that correlated equilibria are more tractable objects than Nash equilibria. From a conceptual standpoint, we connect correlated equilibria to a natural generalization of fixed points, which we call fixed sets. A fixed set of a continuous function $f$ is a nonempty finite set $S$ such that $S \subseteq \operatorname{conv} f(S)$. Our main technical contribution is to prove that computing a fixed set is PPAD-hard even at inverse polynomial precision.
radar.summary_short: We show that computing an approximate correlated equilibrium of a polytope game is PPAD-complete, and thus polynomial-time equivalent to finding a Nash equilibrium. radar.title: MAS-Guard: Unified Guardrails from Individual Agents to Multi-Agent LLM Systems
radar.summary: Agentic AI extends large language models (LLMs) from generating responses to planning and executing complex workflows, substantially expanding their utility while exposing applications to unsafe actions, information leakage, and adversarial manipulation. Multi-agent systems further expand these capabilities through specialization and collaboration, but distributed authority, heterogeneous roles, and opaque or potentially compromised participants make safeguarding even more challenging. Existing defenses address important individual threats but provide fragmented coverage across local execution, system-level interactions, and enforcement mechanisms. We introduce MAS-Guard, a unified framework that closes this gap for safeguarding single- and multi-agent AI applications containing both instrumentable and opaque agents. Within instrumentable agents, the proposed local Agent Guardrail (A-Guard) layer applies task-specific experts to assess agentic events. At the system level, developer-owned Agent Charters and a Control Plane combine deterministic structural checks of routes, agent capabilities, and message formats with semantic assessments of roles and message content. These complementary layers enable enforcement through a shared set of interventions: allow, reflection, confirmation, and block. Evaluated across six benchmarks covering diverse single- and multi-agent scenarios with three agent LLMs from different providers, MAS-Guard reduces the overall attack success rate by 71.5-86.3% relative to unguarded agents, while meeting the utility reference criterion on benign tasks.

radar.title: Posterior-conditioned multi-agent reinforcement learning for adaptive cyber defense
radar.summary: Cyber defense increasingly relies on teams of autonomous agents that must act under partial observability while adversaries shift tactics and objectives over time. Standard multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) methods often overfit to fixed threat models, whereas worst-case robust training can be overly conservative and fail to use observations about the active attack regime. We propose posterior-conditioned MARL, a context-aware framework formulated as a decentralized partially observable Markov decision process (Dec-POMDP). In addition to its local history, each defender conditions its decentralized policy on a shared attack-context belief, a probabilistic representation of the attack regime inferred online from recent multi-agent interaction trajectories. This belief provides a low-dimensional representation of evolving adversarial behavior and enables coordinated adaptation during execution without test-time policy optimization or retraining. We provide a performance analysis that quantifies how errors in the inferred attack-context belief translate into degraded long-term defense performance, clarifying the tradeoff between robustness and adaptivity. Experiments on the Cyber Autonomy Gym for Experimentation (CybORG) CAGE-4 cyber operations testbed show improved mission reward and adaptability, particularly under mixed and switching attack conditions, compared with domain-randomized, worst-case robust, and hierarchical defense baselines.

radar.title: Trust-Weighted Adaptive Consensus: A Resilient Coordination Framework for Next-Generation Large Language Model Multi-Agent Systems
radar.summary: Large language model (LLM) agents have moved from singleturn assistants to persistent, tool-using systems that plan, delegate, and cooperate.This shift has produced an explosion of multi-agent system (MAS) frameworks, interoperability protocols, and orchestration patterns, yet production deployments continue to report failure rates far higher than single-agent baselines.This paper synthesizes the current state of AI agents and multi-agent systems as of mid-2026, organizes the coordination design space into a four-part topology taxonomy, and reviews the emerging empirical literature on why multi-agent systems fail.Building on documented gaps, particularly the absence of adaptive, trust-aware coordination in widely used frameworks.We propose Trust-Weighted Adaptive Consensus (TWAC), a coordination-layer mechanism that combines capability-aware sparse shortlisting, an exponentially-weighted per-agent trust ledger, and uncertainty-gated verification.We evaluate TWAC against round-robin and centralized-auction baselines in a controlled simulation across 500 tasks and 30 independent trials.TWAC improves task success rate while reducing communication overhead relative to full-broadcast coordination and lowering cascading-failure rates by more than an order of magnitude.We conclude with future research implications for trust-based coordination in agentic AI systems.

radar.title: HGRL: A heterogeneous graph-based reinforcement learning framework for robotic swarm applications
radar.summary: Graph neural networks provide a structured approach for representing entities and their relationships in multi-agent systems. In this paper, we propose a heterogeneous graph-based multi-agent reinforcement learning framework, termed HGRL, to support decision-making in robotic swarms. HGRL represents the interactions among agents and environmental entities using heterogeneous graphs. Unlike graph-based MARL methods that retain conventional transition tuples, HGRL encodes state–action transitions as variable-size heterogeneous graph objects and preserves this representation during experience replay and actor-critic optimization. This graph-based formulation allows changes in the numbers and types of agents and environmental entities without restructuring fixed-width experience entries. A graph-based multi-agent soft actor-critic agent is developed to demonstrate HGRL for UAV swarm collaborative navigation, using attention-based graph neural networks to process variable swarm topologies. Under the adopted training setting, the reward and network losses converged within a small number of episodes. Simulation experiments demonstrate successful navigation across different swarm sizes, formations, and planar goal directions. Real-world experiments further demonstrate the transferability of the high-level reference-velocity policy to homogeneous and heterogeneous UAV platforms without fine-tuning. A video of the results is available at https://youtu.be/Ch3ataf1ItQ .
radar.summary_short: Graph neural networks provide a structured approach for representing entities and their relationships in multi-agent systems. In this paper, we propose a heterogeneous graph-based multi-agent reinforcement learning framework, termed HGRL, to support decision-making in robotic swarms.

radar.title: A Blockchain-Driven Stackelberg Game and MILP Algorithmic Framework for Dynamic Pricing in Multi-Agent Microgrid Networks
radar.venue: EAI Endorsed Transactions on Energy Web
radar.venue_raw: EAI Endorsed Transactions on Energy Web
radar.summary: INTRODUCTION: Decentralized coordination and data transparency in multi-agent networks face significant computational and security bottlenecks when performing joint energy and ancillary service trading, particularly due to nonlinear optimization challenges in complex multi-domain environments. OBJECTIVES: This work aims to overcome these bottlenecks by developing an information-driven dynamic pricing framework that enables transparent, autonomous, and computationally efficient multi-agent decision-making. METHODS: The proposed framework integrates Ethereum-based smart contracts deployed on a public ledger to guarantee immutable data interactions and eliminate centralized dispatching. A Stackelberg game model is established to capture upper-lower level decision-making. To solve the resulting highly nonlinear and non-convex game exactly, the problem is transformed into a Mixed-Integer Linear Programming (MILP) model using Karush-Kuhn-Tucker (KKT) conditions and the duality theorem, ensuring exact convergence without approximation errors. RESULTS: Simulation results demonstrate the algorithm’s ability to efficiently find the exact Nash equilibrium, converging to a stable state in approximately 12 iterations. The KKT-MILP framework exhibits exceptional scalability, solving a 50-agent system within just 15 seconds and significantly outperforming traditional heuristic algorithms in computational latency. CONCLUSION: The proposed algorithmic framework mathematically ensures transparent and decentralized decision-making while substantially enhancing computational accuracy and overall economic efficiency of the multi-agent system.
